quote: Ferner: wie modificiren sich diese Bedingungen, wenn man das[?] Modulsystem multiplicirt oder potenzirt.
english: Further: how do these conditions change when one multiplies the module system or raises it to a power?
topic: A dismissive remark on Christoffel's essay on irrational numbers, followed by a research programme on Noether's general theorem about surfaces through given points and curves, membership of a form in a module system, and a link to ideal theory.

triage.modern_statement: Context: Max Noether's Fundamentalsatz (the AF+BG theorem) gives local conditions at the common points of the generators that decide whether a form F lies in the ideal ('module system') M = (f, g, ...). Hilbert's question, restated: given local or primary criteria for 'F ∈ M', what are the corresponding criteria for F ∈ M·N (a product of ideals) and for F ∈ M^k (a power)? Put differently, how does the local or primary structure of an ideal behave when ideals are multiplied or raised to powers? In today's commutative algebra this is the relation between ordinary powers I^k and their local (primary or symbolic) parts. The local parts are the symbolic powers I^(k), and the question is whether I^k = I^(k), i.e. whether I^k is unmixed.
triage.answered_by: There was no single answer. The general framework came from E. Lasker (primary decomposition, Math. Ann. 60, 1905), F. S. Macaulay (The Algebraic Theory of Modular Systems, 1916, which includes the theory of unmixed ideals and of powers of complete intersections), and Emmy Noether (Idealtheorie in Ringbereichen, 1921). Under this framework, membership in any ideal, including products and powers, reduces to membership in its primary components. The specific question about powers grew into the theory of symbolic powers: the Zariski (1949) and Nagata (1962) theorem; Ein–Lazarsfeld–Smith (char. 0, 2001) and Hochster–Huneke (char. p, 2002) on how symbolic powers sit inside ordinary powers; and the 'containment problem', which is still being studied. I found no source that ties any of this work directly to Hilbert's note.

evidence.claim: Max Noether's AF+BG theorem (1873) gives local conditions for a curve to lie in the pencil/ideal generated by two others. This is the starting point of Hilbert's note.

Historical survey (Gray, 'Algebraic Geometry between Noether and Noether'): Lasker, Macaulay and later Emmy Noether wrote at length on generalising Noether's theorem, and Lasker (1905) proved the primary decomposition theorem in that setting.
Bibliographic record: Lasker, 'Zur Theorie der Moduln und Ideale', Math. Ann. 60 (1905), 20–116.
Classical results of Macaulay and Max Noether give conditions for writing a polynomial as a combination of given generators, i.e. ideal-membership criteria.
Emmy Noether's 'Idealtheorie in Ringbereichen' (1921) cites Lasker 1905 and Macaulay, and builds the abstract theory of decomposing ideals.
The Zariski–Nagata theorem [Zar49, Nag62] describes symbolic powers, the 'local' counterpart of ordinary powers.
Ein–Lazarsfeld–Smith (char. 0) and Hochster–Huneke (char. p) proved major containment results between symbolic and ordinary powers, and work on the containment problem continues.

triage.why: The note is one line in a research programme about Noether's Fundamentalsatz. It asks how membership conditions change under products and powers of the ideal. Lasker–Macaulay–Noether ideal theory (1905–1921) settled the structural side: membership reduces to primary components. Macaulay's work covers the well-behaved complete-intersection case. For general ideals, the gap between ordinary and symbolic powers is still an active research area (containment problem, Zariski–Nagata, ELS/Hochster–Huneke). The note is not one of Hilbert's 23 problems or the 24th problem. Confidence is low for two reasons. The sources only establish this as the general line of development; none link the note itself to these results. And because the question is phrased loosely, mapping it onto symbolic powers is an interpretation, not something any source states.
